10.34133/space.0267.title: Identifiable Representation and Model Learning for Latent Dynamic Systems
evidence_paragraphs: When executing tasks in complex environments, an intelligent spacecraft [1–3] may encounter low-level observations such as images or outputs of pretrained neural networks [4,5]. These observations generally do not have any physical meaning, and their relationship is usually highly nonlinear and unknown. But there may exist some high-level latent variables (or latents for short), which can represent these observations, and some invariant mechanisms that can describe the relationship between these latents and exogenous inputs [6,7]. Then, these systems can be regarded as latent dynamic systems [8–11].

In reinforcement learning, representation learning is usually used to abstract low-dimensional representations from high-dimensional observations to promote the sample efficiency and generalization ability [10,12,26]. Approaches include reconstruction-based methods [9–11,32–34], contrastive learning [35], self-predictive representations [36], metric-based methods [37], and so on. However, few of these works consider the identifiability of the learned representations and models. Hence, it is unclear whether the true DGP is reliably recovered.

10.34133/space.0291.title: Review of Autonomous Space Robotic Manipulators for On-Orbit Servicing and Active Debris Removal
evidence_paragraphs: Despite the advancements in these control strategies, conventional controllers remain limited in addressing the coupled dynamics of nonlinear systems, especially as the robot’s DOFs increase. The modeling and implementation of sophisticated control strategies become increasingly complex as system complexity grows. To overcome these limitations, model-free deep reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising alternative. RL eliminates the need for precise dynamic modeling by learning complex control policies directly from interactions. It has demonstrated exceptional success in robotic manipulation, offering a robust solution for handling the intricate dynamics of FFSMs and effectively managing external disturbances.
Beigomi and Zhu [34]	Used reinforcement learning for robotic pre-grasping in microgravity, bridging the sim-to-real gap for robotic grippers.

Another visual-based estimation method leverages deep learning (DL) techniques, which have demonstrated significant potential in space missions. Despite their promise, this approach faces several notable challenges. Planets and stars often serve as background distractors for navigation systems, complicating the task of distinguishing the target. Additionally, the absence of an atmosphere and light diffusion in space creates difficult visual conditions. Strong shadows and highly variable illumination can lead to extreme image contrasts and a low signal-to-noise ratio, further impairing performance.

Sonawani et al. [43] proposed the use of a convolutional neural network (CNN) to uniquely determine the translation and rotation of an object of interest relative to the camera. The primary motivation for employing a CNN model is to support object tracking in space assembly tasks, where traditional feature-based methods may not always be sufficient. A significant advantage of CNN models over feature-based approaches is their adaptability. CNNs can be tailored to track different objects simply by training the model on a sufficiently large dataset that includes the new object, making them a versatile solution for a wide range of applications.

In addition to refining dynamic models, incorporating advanced nonlinear control strategies and leveraging machine learning can further enhance control without relying solely on detailed dynamic models. Machine learning approaches, which do not depend on precise dynamic models when applied to robot control, can enable autonomous intelligent control. As a result, machine learning offers great potential to improve the control capabilities of space robots, enabling more intelligent and adaptable operations. These combined approaches will allow researchers to emulate mission conditions more faithfully, provide deeper insights, and better prepare space manipulators for the unpredictability of space.

In future works, trajectory planning research is expected to increasingly integrate machine learning, marking a significant advancement in intelligent planning methodologies. The incorporation of machine learning and other AI technologies holds the potential to greatly enhance the adaptability, efficiency, and overall intelligence of trajectory planning systems. By leveraging data-driven optimization, these methods can learn from past experiences and continuously refine planning strategies, paving the way for more innovative and effective solutions.

Machine learning also enables trajectory planning systems to adapt to dynamic and uncertain environments, a critical capability for applications such as space robotics, autonomous vehicles, and industrial automation. Furthermore, AI-powered algorithms facilitate real-time decision-making, allowing for trajectory adjustments to handle unexpected changes or disturbances with precision and robustness. Looking ahead, research could explore how machine learning can be seamlessly integrated with other systems, such as compliance control, obstacle avoidance, and multi-objective optimization, to create unified and efficient frameworks. However, while the potential is immense, challenges such as the need for extensive computational resources, ensuring data quality, and maintaining reliability in safety-critical applications must be addressed to fully realize these advancements.

10.34133/space.0255.title: Developing Explainable Artificial Intelligence Models for Space Science Applications
evidence_paragraphs: The integration of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) in space science has ushered in a new era of transparency and reliability in AI-driven applications. This paper delves into the transformative role of XAI in enhancing various aspects of space missions, from satellite imagery analysis to planetary science and human–AI collaboration. The introduction highlights the imperative of explainability in AI, emphasizing the need for transparent and ethical decision-making in high-stakes space missions. In the background, this paper explores the evolution of AI in space science and the emergence of XAI as a critical field. The challenges posed by the complexity of space data and the stringent reliability and safety requirements are examined, underscoring the necessity of robust and interpretable AI systems. The paper discusses various XAI techniques, including model-agnostic approaches like LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) and SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), intrinsic methods such as decision trees, and generalized additive models. Visualization tools for XAI, including feature importance plots and heatmaps, are also discussed, demonstrating their role in making AI decisions more interpretable and actionable. Three case studies illustrate the practical applications of XAI in space science: monitoring deforestation in Earth observation, facilitating discoveries in planetary science, and enhancing human–AI collaboration in space missions. These examples showcase how XAI improves transparency and reliability and enables more effective decision-making. Finally, the paper looks toward the future, discussing emerging technologies in XAI and their potential to revolutionize space science. Integrating XAI, human–AI collaboration, NLP advancements, and quantum computing is a key trend in space exploration.

As AI permeates various sectors, its application in critical fields such as space science has become increasingly prominent. While AI offers transformative potential, its complex and often opaque decision-making processes pose substantial challenges. The imperative of explainability in AI arises from understanding and trusting these systems, ensuring their decisions are transparent, reliable, and ethically sound [8]. Explainability in AI refers to elucidating how AI models arrive at their conclusions. In space science, where missions are high-stakes, and the margin for error is minimal, understanding the rationale behind AI decisions is crucial. Trust in AI systems is fundamental to their adoption and success. When scientists, engineers, and stakeholders can comprehend the decision-making process of AI models, they are more likely to trust and rely on these systems [9]. This trust is essential, particularly in space missions where decisions can have far-reaching consequences. One of the primary reasons for explainable AI (XAI) is error identification and mitigation. AI models, especially those based on deep learning (DL), can sometimes produce unexpected or incorrect results due to biases in the training data or unforeseen circumstances. Explainability allows for a detailed examination of the AI’s decision-making pathway, helping scientists pinpoint the source of errors and implement corrective measures. This capability is vital for ensuring the reliability and safety of AI systems used in space exploration [10].

In the 21st century, they have witnessed an explosion in AI’s application across various space science domains. ML and neural networks became pivotal in analyzing the vast amounts of data generated by space telescopes, satellites, and rovers. These AI systems could identify patterns and anomalies in data far more quickly and accurately than human researchers. For example, the Kepler Space Telescope utilized AI algorithms to identify potential exoplanets by analyzing light curves, substantially speeding up the discovery of new worlds [17]. In recent years, AI has become integral to the planning and executing of space missions. Autonomous systems now control spacecraft during complex maneuvers, such as landing on other planets or docking with the ISS. AI-driven robots, like NASA’s Mars rovers, can conduct scientific experiments and make real-time decisions based on their findings [18,19]. Furthermore, AI is crucial in optimizing spacecraft trajectories, leading to more efficient fuel usage and extended mission lifespans.

One of the critical milestones in the emergence of XAI was the introduction of the LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) framework. LIME allows users to understand the decisions of any black-box model by approximating it with an interpretable model locally around the prediction [28]. This method has been widely adopted due to its flexibility and effectiveness in explaining complex AI systems. Another substantial development in XAI has been the SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) method, which provides a unified approach to interpreting model predictions. SHAP values are derived from cooperative game theory and offer a consistent way to attribute the contribution of each feature to the final prediction [29]. This method has been beneficial in sectors where understanding the precise impact of variables is crucial, such as in medical diagnostics and risk assessment. Regulatory requirements and ethical considerations further underscore the importance of XAI. In many jurisdictions, regulations such as the General Data Protection Regulation in Europe mandate that individuals have the right to an explanation for decisions made by automated systems. This legal framework has accelerated the adoption of XAI techniques, as organizations must ensure their AI systems are not only accurate but also transparent and accountable [30]. Ethically, XAI addresses concerns about bias, fairness, and trust in AI systems. By making AI decisions more transparent, stakeholders can identify and mitigate biases in the data and algorithms, leading to fairer outcomes. Moreover, explainable models enhance trust among users, as they can understand and verify the reasoning behind AI decisions.

Furthermore, while AI has been successfully applied in space science, its usage remains largely restricted to offline data processing rather than real-time onboard applications. This limitation arises primarily from the challenge of adapting DL networks to older spacecraft hardware that needs more performance capacity for basic inferencing. Due to their complex weights and topologies, the memory demands of AI models often exceed the available memory on satellites. Additionally, the computational intensity required for AI inference—demanding numerous operations per second to meet latency needs—is generally incompatible with spacecraft’s limited power budgets and heat dissipation capabilities [36]. Dedicated AI platforms like Myriad2 offer a solution by providing architectures that balance model complexity, processing speed, and power consumption. Effective network selection and model compression strategies can further alleviate memory constraints, as research shows specific neural networks can be compacted without substantial loss of accuracy. Another barrier to adopting AI for onboard applications is the lack of confidence in the “black box” nature of AI models [37]. The unpredictability and difficulty in thoroughly testing these models using traditional methods raise safety concerns, especially given the high cost of failure in space missions. To mitigate risks, AI applications may be restricted to noncritical functions, such as local object detection and classification on sensor data, ensuring that any AI failure impacts only the data quality of specific payloads, not the entire satellite. Finally, training deep networks presents challenges due to the scarcity of datasets, particularly for new missions with novel equipment. Training must often occur on the ground using cloud-based GPUs or specialized hardware, relying on synthetic data, which may not fully replicate actual mission conditions. However, this issue can be mitigated by reconfiguring models during the mission using modern COTS ASICs, as the small file sizes required for such updates are compatible with the uplink bandwidth of small satellites.

LIME is one of the most prominent model-agnostic techniques, which creates local surrogate models to explain individual predictions. When a complex model makes a prediction, LIME perturbs the input data and observes the resulting changes in the output. It then fits an interpretable model, such as a linear regression or decision tree, to these perturbed samples [40]. This surrogate model approximates the behavior of the original model within the vicinity of the specific prediction, offering insights into which features are most influential. This method is beneficial for understanding why a model made a particular decision and for identifying any potential biases or errors in the model. They quantify the contribution of each feature to a particular prediction by considering all possible combinations of features. This method ensures consistency and accuracy in the explanations across different models. Overall, by focusing on local interpretability, LIME provides intuitive, human-readable explanations for complex model predictions, making it an essential tool for debugging models, ensuring fairness, and building trust in AI systems.

An illustrative application of LIME is in the context of positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) imaging, where it helps explain the predictions of ML models [41]. Fig. 1 demonstrates this process in detail. Fig. 1A presents the original PET/CT image, while Fig. 1B displays LIME-generated explanations on the same image. The highlighted regions in red in Fig. 1B indicate the areas with the most substantial influence on the model’s decision-making process. These highlighted areas correlate with features or regions critical to the model’s prediction, such as clinically relevant abnormalities or radiomic patterns, offering profound insights into the model’s reasoning.

LIME operates by perturbing the input image and analyzing the corresponding changes in the model’s output, thereby identifying the regions critical for prediction. In this specific instance, the red-highlighted area in the image may correspond to regions of clinical interest, such as abnormal tissues indicative of conditions like radiation pneumonitis. By associating these critical regions with the model’s predictions, LIME not only enhances interpretability but also aids researchers and clinicians in validating the reliability of the model’s decisions and their alignment with domain knowledge. This example underscores the transformative potential of LIME in enhancing explainability in medical AI applications. Such advancements highlight the critical role of explainability in AI, particularly for high-stakes and sensitive domains like medical imaging and diagnostic tools. By integrating tools like LIME, researchers and clinicians are better equipped to trust, validate, and effectively use AI-driven insights. This focus on explainability not only ensures ethical AI practices but also paves the way for broader adoption and trust in automated decision-making systems.

10.34133/space.0199.title: Communications in Space–Air–Ground Integrated Networks: An Overview
evidence_paragraphs: To deal with the challenges brought by the complex transmission environment changes, numerous studies have been conducted on the end-to-end optimization based on deep learning technologies. To avoid potential computational costs resulting from the direct connection of different artificial intelligence (AI) modules in the training process, investigating neural network-based end-to-end joint optimization methods is necessary [44]. Deep learning can also be combined with massive antennas, and several prototypes further validate the practicality of deep learning at the physical layer [45–47]. Compared with traditional optimization algorithms, deep learning-enhanced resource allocation techniques are more adaptable to complex transmission environments and achieve better performance in communication systems.

Recently, there has been extensive research on the design of beam hopping schemes. In [62], a wireless resource allocation scheme was developed for DVB-S2X to exploit the beam hopping across cells, which could ensure the fairness among beam services and minimize the real-time business transmission latency while maximizing the throughput for non-real-time business transmission. For multi-satellite beam hopping, the authors in [63] introduced a method based on load balancing and interference avoidance. This method could allocate cells to different satellites to balance their traffic load and select beam hopping patterns that meet the spatial isolation condition to avoid intra-satellite and inter-satellite co-frequency interference. Furthermore, slot scheduling was employed to meet the traffic demand of each cell as much as possible. The authors in [64] decomposed the multi-satellite joint beam hopping into satellite-cell assignment subproblem and joint multi-satellite beam hopping pattern design subproblem. In [60], the authors considered the joint optimization of beam hopping and NOMA by adjusting power allocation, beam scheduling, and terminal-time slot assignment. In [65], the authors fully exploited the degrees of freedom in terms of time, frequency, and space, and introduced a dynamic beam pattern and bandwidth allocation scheme based on deep reinforcement learning.

Currently, the UAV trajectory optimization is of special importance to enhance the efficiency of multi-UAVs collaborative and energy consumption optimization. In [76], the authors provided a general definition of the efficiency of UAV communications and investigated the energy efficiency of rate maximization and energy minimization for the case of unconstrained UAV trajectory, and the energy efficiency maximization for the case of the general constraints on UAV trajectory, including its initial/final locations and velocities, minimum/maximum speed, and maximum acceleration. An efficient algorithm based on linear state-space approximation and sequential convex optimization techniques was proposed to find the approximate optimal trajectory. The authors in [77] jointly optimized the UAV trajectory and the transmission power allocation of the source and the UAV relay, through block coordinate ascent and successive convex approximation methods, to maximize the throughput. For multi-UAVs that enabled wireless networks, the authors in [72] jointly optimized the user scheduling and association, trajectories, and transmitted power to maximize the minimum average rate among all users. In [78], the authors formulated multi-UAV trajectory optimization as a sequential decision-making issue and proposed a decentralized deep reinforcement learning algorithm. With the rapid development of machine learning, how to use machine learning to design the trajectories of multiple UAVs is worth further investigation.

Spectrum sensing is an essential component of cognitive radio. It serves as a prerequisite for achieving dynamic spectrum sharing, especially in space-ground networks. Secondary users can detect the spectrum occupancy states with a high probability and accurately determine whether to access a specific frequency band by adopting spectrum detection strategies, which avoids network congestion and mutual interference [84], as shown in Fig. 11. The cognitive radio technology based on spectrum sensing has been extensively studied [85,86], and a series of spectrum sensing algorithms have been developed, such as matched filter detection [87], energy detection [88], and eigenvalue-based detection [89]. Considering the long propagation distance of SAGIN, spectrum sensing is required to be done in low signal-noise ratio (SNR) conditions [90]. In such scenarios, the reliability of traditional spectrum sensing methods will decrease, and a deep learning-based spectrum sensing scheme was developed in [90], the detection performance of which was improved in a low SNR regime. In [91], the authors considered a sensing-based cognitive space-ground network that combined a cognitive space-ground network with distributed cooperative spectrum sensing network to maximize the energy efficiency.

As a further development, AI technology provides jammers with more diverse and intelligent jamming attacks, and jamming intelligence is an irresistible development trend of electronic jamming attacks [134]. In [129], a joint multi-agent anti-jamming algorithm was proposed to obtain the optimal anti-jamming strategy. The authors in [121,134] proposed 2 distinct jamming mitigation solutions based on game and reinforcement learning, respectively. Furthermore, the authors in [135] considered the use of an IRS to enhance anti-jamming communication performance against a smart jammer, which could jointly optimize power allocation and reflected beamforming at the IRS.

Although current research has equipped satellite networks with edge cloud servers to provide computational offloading for remote devices, bringing processing heavy applications to remote areas and ensuring ubiquitous connectivity in future 6G networks, the analysis of the significant data generated by these remote devices remains a challenge [142]. Under the circumstance, satellite-based distributed machine learning can leverage satellite networks for distributed data processing and model training, connecting various spots on the earth through satellite systems, to enable collaborative processing of large-scale data for real-time decision-making analysis. Particularly, utilizing satellite networks enables the integration of dispersed data from around the globe into a unified system, which is critical for investigating and addressing the global issues, such as climate change monitoring and natural disaster prediction [143]. In summary, investigating satellite-based distributed machine learning has the potential for SAGIN to enhance the timely response to emergencies and predictive maintenance applications, and additionally, distributed learning contributes to safeguarding user privacy during data transmission, making it of paramount significance.

10.34133/space.0182.title: Resilience Enhancement and Evaluation Methods for Space–Air–Ground Integrated Networks
evidence_paragraphs: Han et al. [26] proposed a spatial anti-jamming scheme for space-based communication networks in SAGIN. The communication confrontation between the hostile force jammers and the satellite nodes of the space-based communication network was modeled as a Stackelberg hierarchical anti-jamming routing game. A deep reinforcement learning-based routing algorithm (DRLR) was proposed to obtain a subset of available routes by using deep learning techniques to extract the effective environmental features of the highly dynamic space-based communication network. A fast response anti-jamming algorithm (FRA) based on the subset of available routes was proposed to make fast anti-jamming decisions by utilizing reinforcement learning techniques to deal with the interactions between satellites and unknown jamming environments. The satellite nodes of the space-based communication network could adaptively make anti-jamming decisions based on the dynamic unknown jamming environment. The algorithm had lower routing overhead and better anti-jamming performance.

The presence of line-of-sight channels in the air-based communication network in SAGIN exposes the air-based nodes to stronger cochannel air-to-air interference and makes them more susceptible to malicious attacks by ground-based jammers. A large number of air-based nodes compete for limited spectrum resources while fighting against malicious external interference. Traditional anti-jamming techniques at the physical layer of air-based nodes include Uncoordinated Frequency Hopping and Frequency Hopping Spread Spectrum, which tend to have high spectrum consumption and low efficiency in a complex and dynamic spectral environment. Du et al. [27] proposed a decentralized anti-jamming channel access scheme for large-scale noncooperative air-based communication networks using a game-theoretic algorithm. The objective of each UAV-to-UAV (U2U) communication link was to find the optimal channel selection strategy to maximize its throughput while avoiding cochannel interference from other U2Us and malicious interference from hostile force jamming devices. The distributed multi-UAV anti-jamming problem was formulated as a Partially Observable Stochastic Game (POSG). The POSG problem was simplified to a mean-field game, in which each U2U link interacted only with the combined jamming from the neighboring U2U links and the external hostile force jamming devices. An adaptive anti-jamming channel selection algorithm based on mean-field multi-intelligentsia reinforcement learning was proposed, which had superior performance in the case of a large number of UAV nodes in the air-based communication network.

In the reconfiguration phase, after adding new air-based node resources to the air-based communication network, the network topology needs to be dynamically reconfigured in order to restore the communication services of the system quickly and with high quality. Chen et al. [37] investigated the topology reconfiguration of air-based communication networks. By intelligently optimizing the flight trajectories of air-based nodes, optimizing the topology of the air-based communication network, and constructing a dynamic UAV Service Function Chain (SFC), the latency and energy consumption of the UAVs for completing the service were jointly optimized to reduce the latency of the UAVs for completing the communication service. The study saved the UAVs’ energy consumption and maximized the net benefit of the SFC end-to-end communication service. Then, a deep reinforcement learning method was applied to solve the optimization problem. A real-time decision-making algorithm based on deep Q-network for multi-UAV actions was proposed to jointly plan multi-UAV trajectories.

10.34133/space.0278.title: Advancements in Multipath Mitigation for GNSS Receivers: Review of Channel Estimation Techniques
evidence_paragraphs: To address multipath effects at the tracking level, we have categorized the estimation techniques into 2 distinct approaches: static and dynamic. Static estimation techniques, such as ML estimators, rely on efficient maximization strategies over the likelihood function to obtain optimal solutions. These methods perform remarkably well in scenarios with long-delay echoes, outperforming other techniques when prior information is unavailable. On the other hand, adaptive approaches for dynamic channels with continuously changing conditions show promise in incorporating prior channel knowledge and dynamically tracking channel parameters for enhanced multipath mitigation. Although the main focus of this work is adaptive techniques, a section dedicated to popular ML-based methods is presented to contextualize the parameter estimation topic and introduce the more advanced adaptive algorithms. Moreover, with the fast-growing use of machine learning methods, particularly for multipath mitigation in GNSS receivers, a section dedicated to those methods is also presented.

AI technology continues to integrate our lives and industries with advancing data-driven models capable of solving a broad range of tasks nowadays [58]. Given future projections indicating a massive transversal adoption of AI after success in diverse fields [59], the use of this technology in GNSS receivers for multipath mitigation has also been investigated [60–62]. From the receiver positioning layer down to the signal tracking level, the proposed machine learning techniques aim to tackle the limitations of current algorithms that rely on physics-based models. Model-based algorithms generally operate under the assumption of white Gaussian noise and depend on accurate physics-based models. Under complex real-world scenarios, these algorithms can be easily exposed to nonnominal conditions, such as interferences, that may severely degrade their performance [63]. Deep learning algorithms rely on data-driven methodologies rather than intricate, physics-based models. These algorithms process vast datasets to identify patterns and relationships, training multiple layers of a neural network (NN) in a computationally intensive process until satisfactory accuracy is achieved. NNs become particularly valuable when such physics-based models are either unavailable or impractical due to their complexity, the latter being the argument for channels with multipath interference.

The literature on machine learning applied to GNSS continuously grows with experiments on different methods used for the most diverse tasks, such as signal analysis and classification [64–68], environment recognition [69–72], and quality assessment [73–75]. For the problem of multipath interference, the different use cases for machine learning methods include the detection of multipath or signal blockage [76–78], the removal of multipath-induced distortion on the ACF [79,80], and channel estimation [81]. Similar to other MMTs from the literature, machine learning methods can be implemented in several processing stages of the receiver and generally use the same information to perform their task. While observation-level approaches typically use the pseudorange and carrier phase measurements, satellite elevation angles, and SNR [71,76,77,82], tracking-level approaches take the baseband signal samples and the correlation values as input [65,79–81].

A machine learning-based algorithm for multipath estimation and compensation is presented in [81]. A multilayer perceptron (MLP) with a hidden layer size of 8 was designed to receive as input the normalized and phase-corrected correlator results and output the channel profile. The LOS parameters are then fed to the conventional tracking loop to adjust the local replicas. The implementation was performed on the BBP2 GNSS ASIC leveraging from an integrated hardware accelerator correlator bank. Although limited to 2-path channel estimation under “infinite” bandwidth and no correlation peak distortions, the results show a multipath error envelope reduction from 75 m to 1.137 m compared to the traditional wide discriminator.

The work presented in [79] studies the use of deep learning to model the multipath effect on the ACF. The traditional correlation structure was replaced by an NN-based correlator scheme, producing and feeding the usual correlation values to the MLP models for regression and classification blocks, responsible for outputting the multipath-free ACF and a binary label on whether multipath is present or not, respectively. The output of the MLP models is used to calculate a weighted average between the raw ACF and the output of the regression block to produce the estimated ACF, which is then fed to the DLL discriminator. Simulation results show an advantage compared to the wide correlator and no substantial improvement compared to the narrow correlator under multipath interference. An extension of this work was presented in [80], where 2 independent and parallel MLP models for regression receive the correlation result from the convolution layer and output the noise-filtered and multipath-free complex ACF. The model was trained based on a single multipath-ray simulation to learn the properties of the multipath interference, and the results using the simulated multipath channel model from the German Aerospace Center (DLR) show an improvement in robustness to multipath-induced errors compared to the standard correlation for shorter integration times. The DLR multipath channel model was also used in [68] to train both an MLP and convolutional neural network (CNN) to detect the presence of multipath in the ACF. A 2D discrete Fourier transform is applied to the ACF from different Doppler frequencies and used as input for the NNs, which serves as a binary classifier—(0) no multipath or (1) multipath. Tests conducted show that decreasing the number of correlators, especially in the frequency domain, negatively affects the performance of the classifier. Additionally, it was demonstrated that the CNN produced more accurate results than the MLP.

In [84], a distributional loss optimization is used as a soft labeling mechanism for a regression CNN. Multipath parameters are estimated from the correlator output using a CNN for high-level feature extraction and a soft labeling approach, where target distributions are modeled as histograms, improving generalization and accuracy through a novel histogram loss function based on Kullback–Leibler divergence. Experiments demonstrate that this technique outperforms traditional regression methods, even at lower image resolutions, which is especially important for practical implementation in physical receivers with limited hardware. In [78], 2 supervised machine learning methods, SVM and NN, are used for NLOS multipath detection from the features of the multi-correlator ACF shape. The argument is presented that using correlation features extracted by SVM and NN yields a more robust solution to discriminate the NLOS than using SNR information.

The literature on channel estimation using machine learning methods is growing fast, with continuous improvements for complex scenarios as more datasets are generated and available for training. While a general picture of how machine learning methods are used for channel estimation at the correlator level is given with the mentioned works, recent and detailed reviews on machine learning applied to multipath mitigation can also be found in [61,62].

Machine learning methods to mitigate multipath have received particular interest from the scientific community for a few decades. Since then, new models on different architectures have been investigated to mitigate multipath and combat the limitations of physics-based models. While current literature and solutions show that machine learning is a powerful tool for complex problems, the application in GNSS receivers to mitigate multipath is still a topic that requires much attention from the scientific community to overcome current challenges. The dependence on a large volume of data that mainly cover complex scenarios (e.g., multipath-dense, low-SNR conditions) is crucial to guarantee the training of models to prepare them for real-world conditions. Although the experiments presented by most articles report better performance in multipath detection or even interference removal compared to traditional techniques, tests are often limited to controlled environments. Further developments are needed to ensure that exposure to different environments does not affect the reported performance. Additionally, computational complexity will be a determining factor for the mass adoption of these methods for channel estimation and multipath mitigation. In addition to several studies reporting the high-resolution dependence of the ACF, which implies a high number of correlators, the model itself also implies an extra computational cost. As with other techniques, computational demand is a limiting factor when implemented on resource-constrained low-power edge devices.

10.34133/space.0197.title: Progress and Development Trend of Space Backlight Detection Imaging Technology
evidence_paragraphs: In recent years, the rise of deep learning has led to the development of numerous HDR image fusion methods. DeepFuse, a representative baseline method for static HDR image fusion, employs an unsupervised deep learning framework to reduce the need for ground truth images. It trains on a large dataset of multiexposure images to achieve LDR fusion [61]. Additionally, the advent of generative adversarial networks (GANs) has influenced HDR image fusion techniques. Xu et al. [62] introduced MEF-GAN (Multi-Exposure Fusion GAN), which incorporates a self-attention mechanism into the generator to address the pronounced spatial brightness variations in LDR images, enabling long-range dependency learning.
